newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish lower house clears new central bank charter.
newsitem.headline: Polish lower house clears new central bank charter.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament on Friday approved a draft law on the National Bank of Poland (NBP), the central bank, which shields its independence but shifts power to shape monetary policy.

The bill provides for creation of a Monetary Policy Council (RPP), headed by the bank's president, which would collectively decide on interest and exchange rates, levels of market intervention, bank's obligatory reserves and other key monetary policy elements.
Under current law these decisions are up to the central bank's management, led by its president.
In a vote on Friday, the lower house increased the proposed number of the Monetary Policy Council members to nine from the earlier proposed six.
The council members, respected financial experts, would be chosen by the lower house of parliament, the senate and the president.
The draft law, which must still clear the senate and be signed by the president, was approved in a 357 to 0 vote with 14 abstentions.
The bill entrenches the independence of the central bank's president, who, as now, would be appointed by the lower house after a recommendation of the president for six years.
The central bank president could be removed only for health reasons or if convicted of a crime.
Under the bill, the NBP would no longer have to seek parliamentary approval of its annual monetary policy programme.

The Friday vote dispelled concerns that the co-ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) wanted to remove the rightist central bank head Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz before her term ends in March next year.

Opposition fears that the SLD would use its strong position in parliament to appoint the Monetary Policy Council members before the September 21 parliamentary polls did not materialise as the law would come into life from the start of 1998.

The new central bank charter is a compromise between the government and the NBP -- the central bank agreed to the creation of the Monetary Policy Council and the government dropped its plans to strip banking supervision from the NBP.

Banking supervision would remain within the NBP, but would be overseen by a body called the Banking Supervision Commission (KNB), comprised of representatives of the NBP, the finance ministry, the president's office and the Banking Gurantee Fund.
